q.intro.text: A rug is three feet by two feet, so it takes six square feet of fabric. A scaled copy has every length three times as long. How much fabric does the copy take? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one, and watch the rugs move first.

e.step0.text: Every length times three. The copy is nine feet long and six feet wide.

e.step1.text: The length times three. One row holds three rugs. That is three times six, eighteen square feet. But the copy is not full yet.

e.step2.text: The width times three as well. Three rows of three rugs. The row’s eighteen square feet, three times. Eighteen times three is fifty-four.

e.step3.text: Each length gave one factor of three, so the area is times three times three. Three squared is nine. That is nine rugs, fifty-four square feet. Check: nine times six is fifty-four.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why does the copy take nine times the fabric, not three times?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. The length multiplies the area by three, and the width multiplies it by three again.

e.why.k.text: Three times the fabric is just one row of rugs. The copy is three times as long and three times as wide. That makes three rows.

e.why.add.text: Six rugs would leave a gap. Count them. Three rows of three is nine. The factors multiply.

t.intro.text: A photo is four inches by three inches. That is twelve square inches. A print has every length two times as long. The first two steps are done for you.

t.count.text: Now the width doubles too. How many photos fill the print?

t.count.ok.text: Yes. Two rows of two photos. Two times two is four.

t.count.k.text: Two photos fill only one row. That was the length. The width doubles too, so there are two rows.

t.count.no.text: Count the rows, then the photos in each row.

t.area.text: What is the area of the print?

t.area.ok.text: Yes. Four photos of twelve square inches. Forty-eight square inches. And eight times six is forty-eight. It checks.

t.area.k.text: Twenty-four is one row of photos. There are two rows. Four photos of twelve square inches.

t.area.factor.text: Four is how many photos fit, not the area. Each photo is twelve square inches.

t.area.sq.text: That squares the area. Square the scale factor instead. Two times two is four photos of twelve.

t.area.no.text: Four photos, and each one is twelve square inches.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked fifty-four square feet, and you were right. Now you can show why. One factor of three for each length.

q.cb.k.text: At the start you picked eighteen square feet. That is one row of rugs. It scales the length only. The width scales too.

q.cb.add.text: At the start you picked thirty-six square feet. That adds the factors, three plus three. The rows of rugs show they multiply. Three times three.

q.cb.none.text: Every length times k. The area is times k, then times k again. That is k squared.

p.intro.text: Riley scales a triangle by two. The base goes from four to eight, the height from three to six. Riley says: k times k is for rectangles. My triangle’s area just doubles, from six to twelve square units. Is Riley right?

p.test.text: Let’s test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. Four copies fill the big triangle, the middle one turned around. Riley’s twelve is struck out.

p.c2.text: Right. Four copies of six square units. Four times six is twenty-four.

p.c3.text: Right. Doubling the base doubles the area. Doubling the height doubles it again. And one half times eight times six is twenty-four. It checks.

p.no.k.text: That is exactly Riley’s claim. Count the copies in the picture. There are four, not two.

p.no.rect.text: The triangle tiles too. Four copies fill it. The rule is not special to rectangles.

p.no.ex.text: One triangle can’t prove it for every figure. The reason must work for any base and any height.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That’s a proof. Three claims, each with its reason, and the picture backs every one. Scaling by two makes four times the area, for triangles too.
